job_title: Senior Full Stack Developer (Node.js, TypeScript, React.js)

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Most technical recruitment runs on keyword matching: a list of technologies on one side, a job description on the other, and a hopeful guess in between. Doghouse is built on the premise that this is the wrong method — that senior recruiters who genuinely speak tech and ask the right questions will match people to work that actually fits, rather than pushing something close enough. That distinction, between the label and the substance underneath it, is the one my own work has been organised around.

I studied linguistic philosophy before I wrote software, and it left me with a habit I have never quite shaken: before accepting a term, ask what problem it is solving. As an engineer that has mostly meant refusing to stop at the API. I spent five years on the frontend — leading a team of five at TCS, cutting API calls by 40% through better RxJS state handling, delivering enterprise applications with zero WCAG violations at QA — but the more I built on frameworks, the more I wanted to know what they were doing underneath. That took me below the application layer: Node streams and buffers, event-driven architecture, and building an HTTP implementation directly on Node's net module, after working through DNS resolution and TCP-level communication. I am a frontend engineer who deliberately stopped treating the stack beneath her as a black box.

It also shapes how I build. In NewsAlign, a full-stack AI fact-verification system, the interesting problem was not calling a model — it was the gap between retrieval and reasoning: how to retrieve semantically with FAISS and LangChain, how to reason over what came back, and how to keep caching, rate limiting and cost under control. On the same project I reduced the bundle by 68% and moved Lighthouse performance from 73 to 95, with 84% unit test coverage keeping it stable. I have also written a small reactive engine modelled on useState internals, for the same reason I wrote the HTTP layer: the API is not the whole story.

For a Senior Full Stack role in Node.js, TypeScript and React, that combination is less a list of skills than a way of working — enough frontend depth to own rendering, accessibility and performance, enough backend range to reason about APIs, data flow and the runtime beneath them, and the consistent habit of checking an assumption before adding another abstraction. I would bring that to whichever team you place me with, and I would rather be assessed on what I have actually built than on the keywords in a CV. I would welcome a conversation about the roles you are currently working on.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

summary: AI knowledge platform, Senior Frontend Engineer role, scalable AI-driven knowledge interfaces with React/Next.js and performance optimization

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: An AI knowledge platform serving more than two million users keeps two problems in the same room: how the system retrieves knowledge, and how a person reads, trusts and acts on what comes back. The second problem is largely a frontend problem, and it is where I have spent most of my working life. I also noticed that Cursor and Copilot are part of how the team builds. When the mechanical parts of writing code are automated, the remaining work is judgement — knowing which abstraction fits the problem and which one quietly makes it worse. That is the kind of engineering I want to be doing.

The habit of asking what a piece of software was built to solve, rather than accepting it as given, predates my career: I studied linguistic philosophy before moving into engineering, where the equivalent question is what a framework or a rendering strategy is actually there to fix. At TCS I led a team of five developers and owned frontend architecture for enterprise applications, reducing API calls by 40% through RxJS state management, rebuilding rendering paths with code splitting, lazy loading and caching, and delivering UI that held zero WCAG violations at QA. More recently I have worked directly with Next.js App Router, SSR, ISR and React Server Components, which matters here: on a knowledge product, perceived latency decides whether someone keeps using the tool.

The part of TextCortex I would want to be closest to is the knowledge layer underneath the interface. I built NewsAlign, a full-stack fact-verification system using semantic search, FAISS vector retrieval and LLM reasoning, and the insight that stayed with me was that retrieval and reasoning are separate problems — a strong model cannot recover from a badly retrieved context. It also surfaced the constraints a knowledge platform cannot avoid: caching, rate limits, and cost per query. Beside it I built a small reactive JavaScript engine modelled on useState internals, largely out of the same curiosity about what frameworks do beneath their API.

I am applying because this role sits at the intersection of the two directions I have deliberately built towards: senior frontend ownership, and a serious interest in how AI systems retrieve, reason over and present knowledge to people who need to rely on it. I would welcome the chance to discuss what the platform needs next, and where I could take responsibility from the start.

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: This is a one-year fixed-term position, and that detail shapes how I read the rest of the description. A defined window asks something different of an engineer than an open-ended hire: roughly twelve months to become productive inside a high-scale React codebase, ship work that survives production traffic, and leave the code — and the reasoning behind it — in a state the returning engineer can continue from rather than reconstruct. I have worked to that constraint before. My co-op engagement at Datapret was scoped as a fixed term and closed on delivery, and I found it clarifying rather than limiting.

At Zalando's scale, the interesting frontend questions are about where work happens rather than how it looks. What is rendered on the server, what can be cached, what has to arrive fresh, how much JavaScript the browser parses before anything becomes usable — these decide whether an interface feels immediate or heavy, and they are trade-offs rather than framework choices. I studied philosophy before I wrote software, which left me with the habit of asking what problem a concept was introduced to solve before adopting it. I ask that of rendering strategies and state libraries in the same way, and I built a small reactive state engine modelled on React's useState internals to see what actually happens between a state update and a repaint.

That habit has produced measurable results. On NewsAlign, an AI fact-verification project I designed and built, reworking the rendering and caching strategy cut bundle size by 68%, from 941KB to under 300KB, and lifted the Lighthouse performance score from 73 to 95. Professionally, four years at TCS as a Senior Frontend Developer gave me the other half of the picture: leading five developers, owning frontend architecture for enterprise TypeScript applications, reducing API calls by 40% through more deliberate RxJS state handling, and delivering interfaces that passed QA with zero WCAG accessibility violations. The rendering decision and the accessibility of the result matter to me in equal measure, and that is the part of frontend engineering I keep returning to.

What makes this particular role worth pursuing is the combination of scale and a defined horizon. A high-scale environment rewards engineers who measure before they optimise; a one-year term rewards engineers who write for the person who comes next. I would want to contribute early on performance, accessibility and component architecture in the Lounge team, document the reasoning behind decisions as I go, and hand back a codebase that is easier to work in than the one I inherited. I am able to relocate and would welcome the chance to talk about where the team most needs the year to go.

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Bonnie's dashboard and its guest-facing channels are one product seen from two opposite ends. A restaurant operator opens the dashboard mid-service and needs it to be immediate and predictable; a guest meets Bonnie through a WhatsApp widget or a web chat and expects something that behaves like a conversation rather than a form. Optimising for one surface usually lets the other drift, and the part I find genuinely interesting is not either screen on its own but the shared model underneath — which is also where evolving how Bonnie is configured seems to sit. That is the kind of problem I would like to work on.

Professionally, I have spent five years on the frontend side of large applications: at TCS leading a team of five on Angular and TypeScript enterprise work, where RxJS-based state handling cut API calls by around 40%, and later on an accessibility-focused React and TypeScript platform where WCAG compliance improved by 30%. The numbers matter less than what they taught me — performance and accessibility are architectural decisions taken early, not clean-up work afterwards. That is also why I keep moving beneath the framework line. I studied linguistic philosophy before software, and the question I learned to ask about a concept — what problem is it solving, and for whom — is the question I now ask about a config schema or a rendering model.

Two projects come closest to Bonnie's problem. In JobFinder I replaced a ten-question form with a conversational interview: OpenAI interprets free-text answers, SSE streaming keeps the exchange live, and the interview logic, AI integration and profile extraction stay in separate layers so the conversation ends in a structured, editable profile rather than a transcript — configuring something through language while still producing a deterministic structure underneath. In NewsAlign, a RAG-based fact-verification system, the instructive part was less retrieval than constraint: caching, rate limiting and cost control decide whether an LLM feature survives daily use, which is the same arithmetic a guest-facing AI product performs on every message.

What I would bring is discipline about latency, state and accessibility on the dashboard side, and on the channel side a preference for interfaces that fail clearly when the model is slow, uncertain or wrong. Configuration is the area I would most like to help evolve, because it is where restaurant staff, guests and the AI actually meet, and it is usually the layer that ages fastest if it is treated as a settings page rather than a product decision.

summary: Digital identity (eID, signatures), Frontend Engineer role, UX-focused secure scalable frontend systems

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Digital identity products fail in a different way from most software. When a user taps the button to sign, they cannot inspect the cryptography behind it — they have to trust the interface to represent honestly what is being signed and what it means. For products like eID and digital signatures, the frontend is not a decorative layer over the security model; it is where consent actually becomes legible to a person. That makes UX and correctness the same problem, which is precisely the kind of constraint I find worth working under.

My first degree was in philosophy of language, where the working habit was to ask what problem a concept is solving before using it. Digital identity is a rare case where that question is not abstract: identity, signature, and consent are legal and social concepts that have to be made precise enough for software to act on, and then legible enough for a person to trust. I have carried that habit into engineering — I built a small reactive state engine by hand to understand what React's useState is actually doing rather than treating the API as given, and I still spend time below the application layer, in streams, event handling, and network protocols, whenever the abstraction matters to the product. It has been most useful in frontends that have to be trustworthy rather than merely pleasant.

Professionally I have spent around five years in frontend work, most recently with React, Next.js, and TypeScript, and earlier with Angular and RxJS at TCS, where I led a team of five and set frontend architecture for enterprise applications. Accessibility has been a consistent thread: I delivered WCAG-compliant interfaces with zero violations at TCS, and at Datapret I raised WCAG compliance by 30% on a public-facing complaint resolution platform — a product where users had to believe the process was the same for everyone. I am equally comfortable on the performance side: in a personal fact-verification project I brought the bundle from 941KB to under 300KB and the Lighthouse score from 73 to 95, mainly through code splitting, SSR, and caching. The same thinking applies to a signing flow, where a slow or unclear step quietly becomes a reason not to complete it.

What draws me to this role is that identity is a domain where those qualities are not optional. People who cannot see the cryptography need the interface to be clear, accessible, and predictable; institutions need it to be correct. I would like to contribute the frontend engineering I already have — accessibility, performance discipline, and a habit of understanding what sits beneath the surface — and to learn the identity protocols themselves from the people who build them.
